A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Alert research, with Alert★ renamed Alert+. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Alert experiments on 31 datasets, including baseline comparisons, state-space studies and delayed-reward experiments in Section 6 and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on 30 datasets, including retained comparisons and additional controls, sensitivity studies, runtime measurements and qualitative analyses in Section 5 and Appendices B–E.

M1.justification: The default offline DDQN procedure, incremental-cost reward, five-feature state and model-selection strategy are retained; Alert★ becomes Alert+. Appendix D.2 adds optional reward objectives R2/R3 based on hindsight-optimal costs or triggering times, extending the framework's training variants.

E1.justification: Reported benchmark coverage contracts from 31 datasets—20 UCR and 11 Monash—in v1 Section 6.1 to 30—19 UCR and 11 Monash—in v2 Appendix A.1. The omitted UCR dataset is not identified. The additional sensitivity experiments retain these archive-based classification tasks.

E2.justification: The five main competitors are retained. v2 adds Calimera+, which receives Alert+'s features and is directly evaluated in Appendix B.4. The delayed-reward comparison also changes from external competitors in v1 Figure 10 to other Alert reward variants in v2 Figure 13.

E3.justification: v2 adds linear-delay/balanced-misclassification evaluation and experiments varying sampling to 1% and 2%, discount factors, Q-network sizes, SAX/Catch22 encodings and GBM/InceptionTime classifiers. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The original 70/30 split and default MiniROCKET/5% sampling configuration remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's subsampled-series/noise augmentation and delayed-reward checks, v2 adds feature-removal ablations, full-series inputs, alternative rewards, discount/network sensitivity, encoding/classifier/sampling robustness and runtime analysis. The Calimera+ control examines feature-related explanations, while Appendix E adds selected-instance trigger-score and cost analyses at two sampling resolutions.

E5.justification: Both versions already use bootstrap intervals, Wilcoxon tests and Holm correction. v2 Figure 2 explicitly identifies the pairwise plots' bands and bars as 90% bootstrap intervals, previously unspecified for those plots, and Table 2 explains undefined p-values when all observations tie. Neither version specifies repeated-run or seed counts.

E6.justification: Figure 4's mean costs change, including Alert 6.70 to 6.92 and Calimera 7.97 to 8.22; the changed benchmark prevents interpreting these as same-setting deterioration. New findings include no significant separation under linear/balanced costs and improved Calimera+ rankings that generally remain below Alert+. Extensive sensitivity/runtime results are added, while v1's state-space p-value table is removed.

T1.justification: v2 formally defines the new R2/R3 reward objectives and revises Calimera's stated cost difference from minFutureCost_t minus minFutureCost_(t+1) to minFutureCost_(t+1) minus Cost_t. Expanded standard DDQN equations explain the retained algorithm. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central framework and state-design contributions remain. v2 narrows v1's concluding claim of significant superiority for all weighted cost combinations to significant improvements for several trade-offs, and explicitly scopes the abstract's advantage to imbalanced/exponential costs. The state-design study becomes a separately enumerated contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about approximately Markovian states, engineered-feature dependence, training overhead and inability to isolate RL from learning objectives and parameterization. Calimera+ and alternative-cost results refine explanations of the advantage and its boundaries. New sensitivity interpretations and nonstationarity discussion replace v1's concluding emphasis on reduced interpretability.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the default discount factor of 1, ten confidence bins, uniform transition sampling, and settings for added classifier experiments. It reports computation times with five threads and changes the code-access reference from an anonymous repository to the author's GitHub repository. Most original architecture, optimizer and split details are retained.

R1.justification: The literature treatment is substantially refocused from v1's broad handcrafted/RL taxonomy, including shapelets and sequential-testing approaches, toward separable, classifier-agnostic triggering and prior RL reward designs. v2 adds offline-RL, imitation-learning and representation references and explicitly distinguishes Alert from classifier-dependent Earliest/SNP architectures.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Separate problem, information and literature sections become a consolidated background; the methodology gains dedicated pipeline, buffer, reward and training subsections. Dataset and implementation material moves to Appendix A, and the results narrative is reorganized around state design and comparison.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column presentation, redraws the pipeline diagram and removes v1's decision-boundary heatmaps. v1's main and appendix pairwise plots are merged into v2 Figure 2. New state-space/runtime tables and extensive sensitivity/case-study figures are added; the Pareto ordinate is corrected to one minus normalized misclassification cost.

improvement.justification: The feature-matched Calimera+ control, alternative-cost evaluation and classifier/sampling robustness studies substantially strengthen evidence for the central contribution. The linear/balanced null result and explicit attribution caveats make v2's conclusions more defensible, while runtime measurements expose the training-cost trade-off. The unexplained benchmark reduction and removal of earlier state-space p-values weaken continuity, but the gains in controlled evidence and applicability assessment are substantial.
